why: mergeDiaryStates returns local.episode instead of the folded result, so an episode that exists only on the incoming device is silently dropped on a Mac/phone fold — the 0.9.0 '...local' regression that the fold was written to close.
testName: takes an incoming episode when this diary has none

why: Invariant 1 is enforced textually: episode.test.ts walks every non-test .ts/.tsx under src/ (sourceFiles("src")) and requires /prescribedInBed\s*:/ to match episode.ts alone. src/lib/storage.ts is inside that scan scope and already assembles a TreatmentWindow literal in coerceTreatmentWindow, staying off the scan only because it uses property shorthand. Making that key explicit is the realistic drift — a second construction site for a treatment window appears in a diary-hydration module — and it typechecks identically, so no other test changes behaviour.
testName: prescribedInBed: is an object-literal key in exactly one non-test file, episode.ts

why: windowAdherence substitutes report.fellAsleepAt when report.inBedAt is absent rather than returning null. Sleep onset is not time in bed, so adherence would be scored against a clock the patient never reported being in bed at, inflating or inventing a window breach.
find:
if (adherenceUnavailableReason(report, window) !== null) return null;
  const actualInBed = report.inBedAt!;
testName: names missing clocks separately from no window, and never falls back to sleep onset

why: applyBackfill copies incoming.filedLate instead of storing true. A past-date write can then land without the marker, so the raster treats recall as a same-day diary row.
testName: stores filedLate even when the incoming row omitted or denied it

why: The offer list starts at today instead of yesterday, so back-fill can present the current morning as a late night.
testName: never returns today, never a date with an existing report, and never a date outside the window

why: applyBackfill drops the exist-check, so a late filing replaces a completed night with recall. The grid then shows a filled row that is not what it claims to be.
testName: refuses a date that already has a page, even if the caller asks

why: attachRecoveryWrap encrypts a fresh random key instead of the live data key. The recovery door then opens a different room than the password, so a diary sealed before the recovery code existed cannot be read after recovery.
replace: const recoveryWrap = await wrapDataKey(secret, crypto.getRandomValues(new Uint8Array(32)));
testName: the recovery wrap yields the same data key as the password wrap

why: The normalized recovery secret is stored on the lock next to the wrap. Anyone who can read localStorage then has the second door in plaintext.
testName: never writes the recovery code to disk, the vault, a log, or an error

why: Adding a recovery wrap deletes wrap. The password then cannot open a kdf-3 lock, so installing recovery locks the user out of the door they already know.
testName: a lock with recovery still opens with the password

why: Adding recovery strips wrap and leaves kdf 3. A client that has never heard of recovery — the phone that has not updated yet — then treats the correct password as wrong.
replace: return { ...lock, wrap: undefined, kdf: 3, recovery: recoveryWrap };
testName: a client unaware of recovery still opens the lock

why: The recovery wrap is returned without proving it re-opens. An unopenable wrap would still be persisted, and the user would be told they are safe.
testName: proves the recovery wrap opens before returning a lock to persist

why: A wrong recovery code deletes the recovery wrap. One typo then destroys the second door, and a later attempt with the right code has nothing to open.
testName: a wrong recovery code fails cleanly

why: Generating a recovery code also rewrites wrap. The password door then no longer matches what is on disk, which is a silent re-key of the wrapping layer.
replace: return { ...lock, wrap: lock.wrap ? { ...lock.wrap, iv: recoveryWrap.iv } : lock.wrap, recovery: recoveryWrap };
testName: generating a recovery code does not re-key the vault or modify wrap

why: The recovery code is drawn from Math.random instead of crypto.getRandomValues, so it is not a cryptographic secret.
testName: generates the recovery code from crypto.getRandomValues, never Math.random

why: mergeDiskVault keeps the local lock wholesale whenever one already exists, so a stale copy without recovery overwrites a disk copy that has it and the second door is gone after boot.
find:
const here = locks[key];
    locks[key] = here ? mergePasswordLock(here, value) : value;
testName: keeps a disk recovery wrap when local already has the same lock

why: A PUT with a wrong bearer is accepted, so anyone who can guess a 64-hex id overwrites the blob. They still cannot read it, but they can destroy it.
find:
if (!hashesEqual(storedHash, presentedHash)) return empty(403);

  const match = request.headers.get("if-match");
testName: rejects a PUT with a wrong auth key and leaves the stored blob unchanged

why: An update writes without etagMatches, so a stale device overwrites the current blob. The concurrency token exists only as a header we ignore.
testName: rejects a PUT with a stale etag and changes nothing

why: Registration is a bare put. Two devices racing both succeed; the second overwrites the first binding and one auth key is wrong forever.
testName: lets exactly one of two concurrent registrations for the same unseen id succeed

why: The presented bearer is stored next to the hash. A bucket breach then yields a token that overwrites any vault.
testName: stores only the auth key hash, never the raw key

why: GET for a missing account returns 200 and a body, so a probe learns the id is unused and the Worker has started inventing content.
replace: if (!meta) return new Response("no such account", { status: 200 });
testName: returns 404 with no detail for an unknown account

why: The path accepts a UUID again, so lookupId (64 hex) is 400 and the two object kinds no longer share one alphabet.
testName: rejects a malformed accountId before any R2 access

why: A malformed accountId reaches R2. The 0.8.23 study-server traversal was this class of bug.
testName: rejects a malformed accountId before any R2 access

why: PUT JSON-parses the body, so the Worker learns what a diary is and a non-JSON blob is rejected.
find:
const body = await request.arrayBuffer();
  if (body.byteLength > MAX_BYTES) return empty(413);
testName: never decrypts, parses, or inspects the body

why: The Worker imports the diary app, so app dependencies and vault types leak into the edge runtime.
testName: imports nothing from src/

why: A size floor treats a small account-record blob as invalid and a diary blob as valid. The Worker has learned that two kinds of object exist.
replace:
if (body.byteLength > MAX_BYTES) return empty(413);
  if (body.byteLength < 1024) return empty(400);
testName: stores two objects at different ids without a type, size heuristic, or kind branch
